evidence.paraphrase: Śaunaka asks location and manifestation date. Sūta places Vakratunda at the eastern limit, installed by gods/sages/Gaṇas, manifest on Bhādra bright fourth; midday worship gives immense siddhis, beginning/end less. Images lie in each island/region’s east; square field ten yojanas, deity central with Siddhi left/Buddhi right, lion in front, eight siddhis in eight directions, eight Gaṇas and Śiva/Viṣṇu/Sun/Śakti in four directions.

evidence.paraphrase: Brahmā and deities occupy east/behind, Gaṅgā and rivers south, Kāśī and fields west, Vasiṣṭha and sages north. Śeṣa/Nāga kings, Gandharvas, mountains, Siddhas, Apsarases, Vidyādharas and Kinnaras serve joyfully and exchange Vakratunda stories; bathing in the ocean they create tīrthas bearing their names.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa tīrtha bathing fulfils life; pilgrimage gives desired ends; dying in the field gives Brahman state. Distant remembrance gives enduring liberation by śukla-gati; devotees anywhere attain Brahman and purify people by sight. Sūta limits his account: even Śeṣa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Vedas, Skanda and yogins cannot exhaust it, and he repeats Mudgala’s account to Dakṣa.

evidence.paraphrase: Bhārgava sage Ṛcīka grows old through long austerity, sees deer with mates/descendants, desires household life and asks king Gādhi’s daughter. Gādhi demands a thousand dark-eared horses as his established marriage-price. Ṛcīka gets them from Varuṇa and gives them; frightened Gādhi duly marries his daughter to him. Her mother laments, provides goods/clothes and sends her to the forest, where she diligently serves Ṛcīka.

evidence.paraphrase: Pleased by his wife’s good conduct, Ṛcīka uses his own austerity to create a richly adorned forest city with four social classes, servants and wealth, and adopts a youthful form. He enjoys marriage properly, then judges its pleasures small and becomes unattached.

evidence.paraphrase: The queen visits with wealth/clothes and finds a magnificent city rather than the hermitage; a sweeper identifies Ṛcīka’s city and summons her daughter. Seeing the prosperous sage, she tells her daughter to ask him for sons for both women. Ṛcīka prepares two carus/puroḍāśas with Brahmin/Kṣatriya potency and specifies each eater, then leaves for midday rites. The mother orders exchanging their portions; daughter complies, mother returns home, both become pregnant.

evidence.paraphrase: Ṛcīka sees fierce radiance in his wife and asks about Kṣatriya potency. She admits the exchange; he predicts her brother will be an ascetic, her son a fierce bowman. Afraid, she asks a Brahmin son and threatens her life otherwise. He shifts that quality to her grandson, informs Viṣṇu of the pregnancy and effects it through tapas. Jamadagni is born to him; Rāma, best bearer of weapons, becomes Jamadagni’s son. Gādhi’s queen bears Viśvāmitra in ninth month; Gādhi installs his grown son in the kingdom and leaves for austerity.

Viśvāmitra requests Nandinī; refused, he orders her seizure. She destroys the messengers; when men whip her, she creates a great army which destroys the king’s whole army. He returns defeated.

Viśvāmitra recognizes Brahmin power’s superiority and his destroyed weapons.

evidence.paraphrase: Viśvāmitra abandons kingdom, fasts and repeats Gāyatrī by puraścaraṇa for Brahminhood, scorching the world. At10,000 years Brahmā offers a boon; his Brahminhood request is answered with further austerity. Brahmā comes ten times offering another boon, which he refuses. His tapas subjects gods and awes Brahmins into assent to his claimed Brahmarṣi rank; Vasiṣṭha still calls him Rājarṣi. Furious, he repeatedly attempts Vasiṣṭha’s death without success and remains distressed.

evidence.paraphrase: After60 rainless years and terrestrial devastation, Brahmā approaches Sūrya-line king Divodāsa, who left rule and performs devotional tapas for liberation. Brahmā asks him to take Kāśī to save life, promising rainfall if he rules. He first refuses, asking liberation; then compassionately accepts on condition earthly rule excludes gods, while gods/heaven, humans/earth and Nāgas/Rākṣasas/Pātāla keep their domains. He will worship Śambhu as a deity; Brahmā agrees and grants Kāśī.

evidence.paraphrase: Brahmā takes Śiva with gods/sages to Mandara to grant Marīci a boon, warning the ascetic will die otherwise. Marīci asks liberation; suffering from tapas he relinquishes life, obtains Śiva’s likeness and reaches Kailāsa. Brahmā then asks Śiva to remain at Mandara, explaining Divodāsa’s condition for drought relief and asking pardon. Śiva agrees with a sigh and stays with Pārvatī/Gaṇas.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva laments that Avimukta was taken from him and his Viśvanātha title is powerless. Recognizing obstacle and removal of pride, he resolves refuge in Vighnarāja and meditates on Gaṇeśa at the mountain for Kāśī. Personified Kāśī hears his departure, loses pride and meditates on Vighneśa for Śiva. Divodāsa’s righteous reign restores rain, joy and sinless observance of social duties.

evidence.paraphrase: Healthy people, fruitful trees, abundant cow milk, sacrifices and svāhā/svadhā please gods/ancestors. Divodāsa’s daily circuit worships Dhundhi first, then Viśveśvara, Jagadambā, Kāśī, Maṇikarṇī, Bhāgīrathī, Mādhava, Jaigīṣavya cave, Kālabhairava and Daṇḍapāṇi. He makes people perform this and punishes the unrighteous;80,000 years pass without even slight sin entering.

evidence.paraphrase: Gods resent loss of earthly sovereignty and scheme against the king. Indra orders Agni to withdraw outward fire; people seek Divodāsa, who assumes fire-form by tapas everywhere on earth. As other gods withdraw he supplies their functions through forms including Vāyu, unknown to the people. Gods ask Brahmā what to do; he sends them to request restored places. They praise Divodāsa, he praises them and restores their offices, remaining in one human body. Agni and others resume their places. The transcription misnumbers sequential63 as33.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva grieves that the righteous tapas-powered king cannot be displaced. Gods/sages offer to lure citizens by siddhis so their sin falls on king, then Śiva can take Kāśī. Their many forms and siddhis fail for a year because citizens remain righteous. Śiva’s further dispatched Bhairavas, Ādityas, Vasus, sages, Yoginīs and Gaṇas fail. Brahmā is sent and performs ten Aśvamedhas, then becomes quiet.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva meditates on Vighnarāja for one year, asking freedom from obstacles and separation. Seeing complete humility, Vakratunda manifests lion-mounted, four-armed, noose/goad/boon/fearlessness, red elephant face, great belly, Siddhi/Buddhi, Śeṣa at navel and Cintāmaṇi. Śiva worships/hymns creator/preserver/destroyer and causal/transcendent forms, seeks inseparable Kāśī, and recalls an earlier promise to appear in son-relation on remembrance. Vakratunda promises hymn recitation/hearing gives siddhis, enjoyment/liberation and all other requests, restoring Avimukta meaning.

evidence.paraphrase: Vakratunda creates a beautiful all-knowing radiant Brahmin from his body and directs him to delude Kāśī citizens and Divodāsa and restore rule to Śiva. People will call him Dhundhi the astrologer and honor him, his descendants likewise. The Brahmin bows, circles and goes remembering Gaṇeśa. Vakratunda commands Viṣṇu to enter Kāśī in Buddhist form and corrupt the already-deluded city. Viṣṇu obeys; both accomplish the ordered delusion and corruption.

evidence.paraphrase: Kāśī meditates for a thousand years; lion-mounted adorned Gaṇeśa arrives. She rises, bows, worships and hymns infinite/formless/formful, Siddhi/Buddhi lord, protector and obstacle-giver to nondevotees. Afflicted separation makes her Avimukta name empty; she asks Śiva’s sight. He promises return, meaningful Avimukta name, hymn that removes separation, desired ends and Brahman state to faithful reciters/hearers. He disappears; she keeps meditating, awaiting the time.

evidence.paraphrase: Dhundhi astrologer instantly deludes the city; Viṣṇu as Buddha then corrupts it. Divodāsa is instructed by Dhundhi and gives up rule through the Buddhist figure, awaiting Śiva. Both summon Śiva, who leads worshipped Gaṇeśa into Kāśī as first resident, then enters with gods/sages. Kāśī bows to both; gods/sages take places and Śiva grants Divodāsa liberation.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa tells Śiva he restored Kāśī and will return to his own abode, visible again on Śiva’s remembrance; he disappears with Dhundhi Brahmin. Śiva creates and installs his image with gods/Brahmins, worships and announces: worship Dhundhi before pleasing Śiva to receive enjoyment/liberation, otherwise not; Vakratunda gives Kāśī-residence fruit. Naming the discovered Vedic root Dhundhirāja, Śiva credits him with four human aims and devotes daily service.

Distant remembrance gives enduring liberation by śukla-gati; devotees anywhere attain Brahman and purify people by sight. Sūta limits his account: even Śeṣa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Vedas, Skanda and yogins cannot exhaust it, and he repeats Mudgala’s account to Dakṣa.

Śaunaka asks what followed Mudgala’s discourse to Dakṣa. Dakṣa asks the detailed Dhundhirāja incarnation and how Vakratunda is born from Śaṅkara’s body. Mudgala introduces an old Gaṇeśa account Yājñavalkya taught Kauśika, illuminating Brahminhood.

Bhārgava sage Ṛcīka grows old through long austerity, sees deer with mates/descendants, desires household life and asks king Gādhi’s daughter. Gādhi demands a thousand dark-eared horses as his established marriage-price. Ṛcīka gets them from Varuṇa and gives them; frightened Gādhi duly marries his daughter to him. Her mother laments, provides goods/clothes and sends her to the forest, where she diligently serves Ṛcīka.

Pleased by his wife’s good conduct, Ṛcīka uses his own austerity to create a richly adorned forest city with four social classes, servants and wealth, and adopts a youthful form. He enjoys marriage properly, then judges its pleasures small and becomes unattached.

The queen visits with wealth/clothes and finds a magnificent city rather than the hermitage; a sweeper identifies Ṛcīka’s city and summons her daughter. Seeing the prosperous sage, she tells her daughter to ask him for sons for both women. Ṛcīka prepares two carus/puroḍāśas with Brahmin/Kṣatriya potency and specifies each eater, then leaves for midday rites. The mother orders exchanging their portions; daughter complies, mother returns home, both become pregnant.

Ṛcīka sees fierce radiance in his wife and asks about Kṣatriya potency. She admits the exchange; he predicts her brother will be an ascetic, her son a fierce bowman. Afraid, she asks a Brahmin son and threatens her life otherwise. He shifts that quality to her grandson, informs Viṣṇu of the pregnancy and effects it through tapas. Jamadagni is born to him; Rāma, best bearer of weapons, becomes Jamadagni’s son. Gādhi’s queen bears Viśvāmitra in ninth month; Gādhi installs his grown son in the kingdom and leaves for austerity.

King Viśvāmitra hunts, grows hungry/thirsty and reaches Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage. Vasiṣṭha feeds king and army by the cow’s power. Viśvāmitra requests Nandinī; refused, he orders her seizure. She destroys the messengers; when men whip her, she creates a great army which destroys the king’s whole army. He returns defeated.

Viśvāmitra leaves rule to ministers and propitiates Śaṅkara in forest. At100 years Śiva grants complete missile knowledge. He returns, attacks Vasiṣṭha and hermitage with fire missile and other weapons. Vasiṣṭha’s Brahmadaṇḍa destroys every missile and defeats him; he flees. Brahmins comfort Vasiṣṭha. Viśvāmitra recognizes Brahmin power’s superiority and his destroyed weapons.

Viśvāmitra abandons kingdom, fasts and repeats Gāyatrī by puraścaraṇa for Brahminhood, scorching the world. At10,000 years Brahmā offers a boon; his Brahminhood request is answered with further austerity. Brahmā comes ten times offering another boon, which he refuses. His tapas subjects gods and awes Brahmins into assent to his claimed Brahmarṣi rank; Vasiṣṭha still calls him Rājarṣi. Furious, he repeatedly attempts Vasiṣṭha’s death without success and remains distressed.

Yājñavalkya, explicitly arisen from Brahmā’s limb, visits. Viśvāmitra bows, worships and says birth, study and austerity bear fruit through seeing him; he asks the visit’s purpose and offers obedience as his servant.

Yājñavalkya came only because he knew Viśvāmitra’s grief, promises to remove it by reasoned knowledge, and hears the denied boon and Vasiṣṭha’s Rājarṣi address. He promises Brahmarṣi rank after relinquishing pride/envy and offers the Kāśī–Viśveśvara story: their inseparability even at dissolution produces pride and a separating obstacle. Viśvāmitra asks its nature.

After60 rainless years and terrestrial devastation, Brahmā approaches Sūrya-line king Divodāsa, who left rule and performs devotional tapas for liberation. Brahmā asks him to take Kāśī to save life, promising rainfall if he rules. He first refuses, asking liberation; then compassionately accepts on condition earthly rule excludes gods, while gods/heaven, humans/earth and Nāgas/Rākṣasas/Pātāla keep their domains. He will worship Śambhu as a deity; Brahmā agrees and grants Kāśī.

Brahmā takes Śiva with gods/sages to Mandara to grant Marīci a boon, warning the ascetic will die otherwise. Marīci asks liberation; suffering from tapas he relinquishes life, obtains Śiva’s likeness and reaches Kailāsa. Brahmā then asks Śiva to remain at Mandara, explaining Divodāsa’s condition for drought relief and asking pardon. Śiva agrees with a sigh and stays with Pārvatī/Gaṇas.

Śiva laments that Avimukta was taken from him and his Viśvanātha title is powerless. Recognizing obstacle and removal of pride, he resolves refuge in Vighnarāja and meditates on Gaṇeśa at the mountain for Kāśī. Personified Kāśī hears his departure, loses pride and meditates on Vighneśa for Śiva. Divodāsa’s righteous reign restores rain, joy and sinless observance of social duties.

Healthy people, fruitful trees, abundant cow milk, sacrifices and svāhā/svadhā please gods/ancestors. Divodāsa’s daily circuit worships Dhundhi first, then Viśveśvara, Jagadambā, Kāśī, Maṇikarṇī, Bhāgīrathī, Mādhava, Jaigīṣavya cave, Kālabhairava and Daṇḍapāṇi. He makes people perform this and punishes the unrighteous;80,000 years pass without even slight sin entering.

Gods resent loss of earthly sovereignty and scheme against the king. Indra orders Agni to withdraw outward fire; people seek Divodāsa, who assumes fire-form by tapas everywhere on earth. As other gods withdraw he supplies their functions through forms including Vāyu, unknown to the people. Gods ask Brahmā what to do; he sends them to request restored places. They praise Divodāsa, he praises them and restores their offices, remaining in one human body. Agni and others resume their places. The transcription misnumbers sequential63 as33.

Śiva grieves that the righteous tapas-powered king cannot be displaced. Gods/sages offer to lure citizens by siddhis so their sin falls on king, then Śiva can take Kāśī. Their many forms and siddhis fail for a year because citizens remain righteous. Śiva’s further dispatched Bhairavas, Ādityas, Vasus, sages, Yoginīs and Gaṇas fail. Brahmā is sent and performs ten Aśvamedhas, then becomes quiet.

Śiva meditates on Vighnarāja for one year, asking freedom from obstacles and separation. Seeing complete humility, Vakratunda manifests lion-mounted, four-armed, noose/goad/boon/fearlessness, red elephant face, great belly, Siddhi/Buddhi, Śeṣa at navel and Cintāmaṇi. Śiva worships/hymns creator/preserver/destroyer and causal/transcendent forms, seeks inseparable Kāśī, and recalls an earlier promise to appear in son-relation on remembrance. Vakratunda promises hymn recitation/hearing gives siddhis, enjoyment/liberation and all other requests, restoring Avimukta meaning.

Vakratunda creates a beautiful all-knowing radiant Brahmin from his body and directs him to delude Kāśī citizens and Divodāsa and restore rule to Śiva. People will call him Dhundhi the astrologer and honor him, his descendants likewise. The Brahmin bows, circles and goes remembering Gaṇeśa. Vakratunda commands Viṣṇu to enter Kāśī in Buddhist form and corrupt the already-deluded city. Viṣṇu obeys; both accomplish the ordered delusion and corruption.

Kāśī meditates for a thousand years; lion-mounted adorned Gaṇeśa arrives. She rises, bows, worships and hymns infinite/formless/formful, Siddhi/Buddhi lord, protector and obstacle-giver to nondevotees. Afflicted separation makes her Avimukta name empty; she asks Śiva’s sight. He promises return, meaningful Avimukta name, hymn that removes separation, desired ends and Brahman state to faithful reciters/hearers. He disappears; she keeps meditating, awaiting the time.

Dhundhi astrologer instantly deludes the city; Viṣṇu as Buddha then corrupts it. Divodāsa is instructed by Dhundhi and gives up rule through the Buddhist figure, awaiting Śiva. Both summon Śiva, who leads worshipped Gaṇeśa into Kāśī as first resident, then enters with gods/sages. Kāśī bows to both; gods/sages take places and Śiva grants Divodāsa liberation.

Gaṇeśa tells Śiva he restored Kāśī and will return to his own abode, visible again on Śiva’s remembrance; he disappears with Dhundhi Brahmin. Śiva creates and installs his image with gods/Brahmins, worships and announces: worship Dhundhi before pleasing Śiva to receive enjoyment/liberation, otherwise not; Vakratunda gives Kāśī-residence fruit. Naming the discovered Vedic root Dhundhirāja, Śiva credits him with four human aims and devotes daily service.
